title: Snack Independence & Pouring
strapline: Pour your own milk, butter your own toast, choose when you're hungry — real jobs, real jug, real spills, real pride.
intent: Give toddlers genuine ownership of snack — pouring their own drink, serving their own food, clearing their own plate.
Develop the hand control and coordination of pouring from a small jug, spreading with a knife and using a spoon and open cup.
Grow independence, decision-making and body-awareness as children choose when they are hungry and how much they need.
Build social skills and language around a shared table — passing, asking, waiting, chatting together.
Accept the spills as part of the learning, with a cloth to hand and no fuss, so children keep having a go.
implementation: Set up a rolling snack table with small, child-sized jugs of milk or water, real crockery, and food children can serve themselves.
Offer real, safe tools — a small jug part-filled so spills stay small, a child's knife for spreading, tongs for fruit.
Keep a cloth and a dustpan within the children's reach so clearing up a spill is part of the job, done calmly by them.
Let children choose when to come to snack within a window, reading their own hunger rather than a whole-group call.
Sit alongside, model 'please pass', pour and spread yourself, and celebrate the careful pour and the wiped-up spill alike.
key_questions: How full will you fill your cup — shall we stop before the top?
Can you spread the butter right to the edges?
Are you feeling hungry, or shall you come back later?
Oh, a little spill — where's the cloth?
Could you pass the fruit to your friend?

impact.text: Toddlers feed themselves with a spoon, drink from an open cup and manage the spills that come with learning.
A child pours their own drink and serves their own food — 'me do it!' — proud to manage snack independently.
Pouring, spreading and serving their own snack, children take real steps towards looking after themselves.
Around the shared table children pass, ask and chat, playing and talking alongside their friends.

enhancements: Small, child-sized jugs part-filled so a spill is only ever a little one.
A snack self-service station with tongs, a butter knife and a name-card sign-in.
A cloth, dustpan and drying rack at child height for clearing up independently.
A 'how many' picture prompt so children serve themselves a sensible amount.
A real vase of flowers or a tablecloth to make the snack table a place worth caring for.

playing_exploring: Children explore pouring, spreading and serving as real, hands-on jobs.
The jug, the knife and the cup are learned through doing, spills and all.
active_learning: Toddlers persist at the careful pour, refining the tip and the stop until the cup fills without overflowing.
creating_thinking: Children judge how full, how much and when they are hungry, making real decisions about their own snack.
